candidates.text:
For crypto founders, the biggest lesson from @fomo and @Pumpfun ascendance is that the distribution model of the last 5 years for apps is moot.

Web3 is dead, wallet connect is dead, dApps are dead.

The new plan is vertically integrated mobile: hide the crypto mechanics entirely. Single balance across chains, integrated onramp (Apple Pay is king), no bridges, no seed phrases or private keys (sign in with Google or X).

For wallet apps themselves, this presents an existential crisis. The user demands simplicity & the feeling of safety. In the past, your wallet was a gateway to crypto. Now, I hold a deposit in each app I use and I don't yet care if they talk to each other.

As always, we go through bundling and unbundling cycles. If Phantom and Jupiter and Metamask were bundling, we are now seeing a great unbundling.

This is Big Company Syndrome. When people like Nikita become entrepreneurs, they realize that they were counting on resources that they took for granted. 

For example. I've met quite a few ex googlers who built startups as if a) the product had been automatically validated and b) they had a guaranteed audience. This is true at Google, and most of the work that's cut out for you at a startup.

Here, @nikitabier thinks "everyone" overthinks marketing, because of how easy it is to announce a new feature to your millions of faithful users. And 99.99% of those he mocks are desperately trying to get attention. Any attention whatsoever, in a world that's constantly barraging all of us with shiny stuff. He is so removed from the struggle of getting noticed that he cannot put himself in the shoes of the average product launcher.

If you leave a big company to start a startup, never forget this. Attention is everything these days.

candidates.text:
exactly a year ago, we fired our CTO. it remains the single most important risk we took for @project_minimi .

some backstory-

on the 2nd of september, after months of compliances and waiting, our investment papers were finally ready. we celebrated that night!

all that remained was for our CTO to put his signature on a document. it was just one click and the money would have been wired.

instead the next morning - he asked for two weeks. not to finish something, not for an emergency - but to make up his mind about whether he wanted to work with us at all. 

this from someone who had been working with us for 18 months. and he had already taken 2.5 months off in the previous 8 months, while my co-founder and i had moved from mumbai to bangalore with barely anything left, holding the team together.

we told him to take his fifteen days. but somewhere in that conversation, we had already made our decision - because a person who can watch his own team gasping for oxygen and still ask for time to think was never going to build this with us.

and since we are not liars, we told the investor exactly what had happened. the investment was cancelled.

what followed was the hardest stretch of this company. we were one-feet in grave already. we were having arguments everyday. our team morale was at an all time low. we couldn’t eat well or sleep well. our now closest well-wishers had seen all of this.

every morning we woke up - anxiety would just find its way and creep in. the morning alarm became a terrorizing call. it was excruciatingly hard on us. our family too were starting to lose hope - and had asked us to return.

during this time I got a job offer from a competitor and i said no to them the same day. i broke my SIP. my co-founder took a loan. and we did the only thing we knew how to do, which was to keep building.

the math had been simple all along: without our CTO, we might not make it. with him, we definitely would not.

a year later, minimi is alive. playing safe was the only path that would have killed us.

TL;DR

tough decisions are excruciating at first but also make the most sense in hindsight. firing our CTO was the best decision we had taken - even if for a while it meant that we might die. 

@project_minimi is a baby born in the storm

candidates.text:
It's actually very common to go from poor to rich without ever experiencing true wealth, because people get addicted to what they know, and the poor and the rich often have a lot in common:

- one is busy all the time because they have no other choice; the other is busy all the time because they don't know what they would do with more freedom (which is something that they've never tasted and are subconsciously afraid of grabbing when it's within their reach.)

- one is obsessed with money because they are constantly in survival mode; the other is obsessed with money because before they knew it, they started playing a game that maximizes status, influence, opportunities, whose money is the fuel.

- one is insecure about what they truly want to do in life because they've never had the chance to experience much besides the small town where they come from; the other is insecure about what they truly want to do in life because it would be a shame to interrupt their hustling career and stop "winning."

- one is struggling with their relationships because they cannot afford to become and maintain a healthy, high-energy, happy version of themselves; the other is struggling with their relationships because they use the same mindset and principles to deal with their problems at work and in private, and that's generally a bad idea to deal with your family and friends the same way you deal with your business partners and coworkers.

The most important part of the journey toward wealth is relearning who you are: if you obsess about the wrong metrics, all you will achieve is converting a certain type of poverty into another type of poverty (that is indeed more widely approved by the rest of society), but it won't make you feel like you are living a life of abundance, it won't make you feel wealthy.
